summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app I use myself, and the more interesting recent work has been less about new features than about a category of bug I keep tripping into: something that passes every test and is still wrong. A dedupe function was comparing IDs instead of the text shown on screen, so nearly half the conversation practice boards quietly offered four copies of the correct answer — no way to get it wrong, and nothing red in the test suite to catch it. A service worker cached "any successful page load" under one key, which was harmless until I added a second static page to the site and the app shell started getting overwritten by it. Neither failure looks like a bug in the code that has it; they look like a bug in the code that reads it later.

That pattern turned into something closer to a discipline: when a guard fires, don't just fix the row it caught, ask what else shares its source. One case: a scheduling rule flagged a single mistranslated word pair (AM/PM confusion in a time-telling drill), and tracing it back showed the same bad data feeding eight other sentences that the check hadn't touched. Fixing the one row would've shipped the other eight.

I also put together a short bilingual send-off for some Japanese colleagues — a spoken piece and a written note, published on a small stand-alone page. The interesting failure was technical, not linguistic: it worked fine in my editor's preview and broke on an actual phone. The audio was embedded as base64 inside one big HTML file, which iOS Safari won't play reliably, and the page itself had no viewport metadata so Safari rendered it zoomed out like a desktop site. Fix was mundane — real audio files, a real HTML wrapper — but a good reminder that "works when I preview it" and "works on the device it's for" are different claims.

Alongside that, I keep a small stable of home-server tooling (an agent that runs my Docker stack, a broker that time-shares a single GPU across a handful of local models) that mostly stays out of the spotlight, except when something breaks in a way worth remembering: a backup job that silently stopped running for months because a directory-existence check was written for a disk layout that no longer existed. The fix was a few lines; the actual takeaway was to add a deadman's switch that pages me if the backup doesn't run, instead of trusting the script to fail loudly.

highlights.oneLiner: Building Keikochō, a self-use Japanese learning app; recent focus on quiet-failure bugs
